newsitem.title: USA: Muni issuers mixed on new Moody's ratings.
newsitem.headline: Muni issuers mixed on new Moody's ratings.

text.p: Issuer reaction was mixed Tuesday to Moody's Investors Service's announcement it will apply its new expanded rating designations to all long-term debt.

The rating designations, which add the numerical modifiers of "2" and "3" to Moody's ratings of B and above, were previously implemented for health care, higher education, and not-for-profit issuers, as well as state revolving fund programs.
The rating agency said Tuesday it will immediately assign the ratings to new long-term debt. Application of the new designations to already rated debt will take place over time, the agency said.
"Moody's is conducting their business," said Frank Hoadley, Wisconsin's capital finance director, who has raised concerns in the past about "uncertainties" the new rating scale would create.

Walter Knorr, Chicago's chief financial officer, said he has requested a meeting with Moody's next week to determine where the city's general obligation rating of single-A would fall under the new system.
Knorr said that was important given the fact Chicago has planned to seek a rating upgrade from Moody's for an approximately $70 million GO bond issue scheduled for sale early next month.
"We're certainly not going to be happy if they say we're an A3," Knorr said. " I think (the city) is a solid A."
Michigan Treasurer Doug Roberts said he is taking a "wait and see attitude" on the new rating designations.
"Any rating is as good as how well the rating agency performs," he said.

One market watcher said the real test of the new Moody's ratings will come from investors. The distinction between, say, an A1 and an A2 rating is only meaningful if the market charges appreciably different prices for the two securities, she said.
Two large California issuers said they were not aware of the expanded rating scale.
"I haven't been told," said the public finance director for one large California county. "I don't have a reaction yet. I have to figure out what it all means."
George Leung, a managing director at Moody's, said that the rating agency had announced last year that the new rating system may be applied to all municipal issuers at some time.
"Clearly investors have reacted favorably, expressing interest in the '2's' and '3's'," he said. "And here going forward we will be discussing with issuers their rating modifiers."
Lueng said high-profile and state issuer ratings should be incorporated into the new system by year end.
